slides.heading: What this course is
bullets: Instructional design: the systematic process of analyzing needs, designing and developing instruction, and evaluating whether it worked
Eight modules following the ADDIE arc, treated critically
Two case analyses and a complete instructional plan of your own
slides.narration: Welcome to ID 553, Introduction to the Principles of Instructional Design. I'm David Awoyemi. Instructional design is the systematic process of analyzing learning needs, designing and developing instruction, and evaluating whether it worked. Over eight modules we'll follow that arc, analysis, design, development, implementation, and evaluation, while questioning it along the way. You'll analyze two realistic design cases, and you'll produce a complete instructional plan for a real problem of your choosing.

slides.heading: Who this course is for
bullets: Teachers who want to design more deliberately
Trainers and faculty developers who build courses and workshops
Technologists and media specialists who work with subject-matter experts
Graduate students preparing for advanced ID work or research
No prior ID coursework assumed
slides.narration: This course is for teachers who want to design instruction more deliberately, for trainers and faculty developers who build courses and workshops, for technologists who work alongside subject-matter experts, and for graduate students heading toward advanced coursework or research. No prior instructional design coursework is assumed. What I do assume is that you'll bring a real instructional problem to work on.

slides.heading: The design project runs through the course
bullets: Choose one instructional problem in Module 1 and keep it
Real, bounded, with learners you can talk to
Assignments 5, 6, and 7 all apply to this one problem
Too large: 'a course on leadership'. Right-sized: 'teaching new tutors to run a 30-minute writing conference'
slides.narration: In module one you'll choose an instructional problem and keep it for the whole course. Good problems are real, bounded, and involve learners you can actually talk to: a unit in your classroom, an onboarding topic at work, a skill your colleagues keep asking about. The learner analysis, the task analysis, and the instructional plan all apply to this one problem. Choosing something too large, like a course on leadership, makes every later assignment harder. Choosing something concrete makes them easier and more useful.

slides.heading: The weekly rhythm
bullets: Read the module pages and linked readings
Check your understanding with the knowledge check (retakes allowed)
Discuss by midweek; reply by the end of the module
Produce the module assignment
Plan on 6 to 8 hours per module
slides.narration: Each module follows the same pattern. Read the pages and any linked readings, and take notes in your own words. Check your understanding with a short, low-stakes quiz you can retake. Post in the discussion by midweek and reply to peers by the end of the module; the discussions are where the field's judgment calls get argued out, so treat them as seminar rather than a box to tick. And produce the assignment. Plan on six to eight hours per module.

slides.heading: Grading and expectations
bullets: 800 points: two case analyses (200), learner and task analyses (150), instructional plan and evaluation (275), reflections (100), models assignment (50), participation (75)
APA 7th edition; cite the readings
AI tools: fine for brainstorming and clarity; disclose use; never submit AI text as your analysis
One 48-hour extension on request; email idawoyemi@crimson.ua.edu
slides.narration: The course is worth eight hundred points. The two case analyses are two hundred, the learner and task analyses one hundred fifty, the instructional plan with its evaluation and reflection two hundred seventy-five, and the rest comes from the models assignment, the course reflection, and participation. Use APA seventh edition and cite the readings. You may use generative AI tools to brainstorm, outline, and check clarity, and you must disclose it; you may not submit AI-generated text as your analysis or reflection, because those are the evidence of your thinking. One forty-eight-hour extension is available on request. Post logistics questions in the pinned Questions thread, and email me for anything private. Let's get started.
